title: Why Bierzo tastes the way it does

lede.text: Bierzo sits in a mountain-ringed basin where the ocean and the interior meet. Its vines get more rain than most of inland Spain, and more than 300 hours of sun a month in midsummer.

chapters.title: A basin behind the mountains
paras: Bierzo is one tectonic basin, a hoya, formed when the Alps were rising. A ring of blunt, flattened mountains surrounds it, with isolated quartzite crests poking out. Below them, rivers have cut deep, narrow gorges.

The vines grow on gentle terraces, on half-terraced slopes and on steep ground, from 355 m to 1,200 m. Most of the vineyard lies between 400 m and 800 m, and the vines face every direction. Vines above 1,000 m make wines that are very fresh and lively.

fly.label: The Bierzo basin
fly.caption: One tectonic basin ringed by mountains, with vines from 355 m to 1,200 m.

chapters.title: Ocean and interior in one valley
paras: The mountain ring gives the basin its own climate, a mix of the oceanic (mild and wet) and the continental (cold and dry). It resembles the Spanish interior, but its winter minimums are higher.

The average year is mild, at about 12.3°C. Winters are cold, and fog often causes temperature inversions. Summers are mild, though very hot days are not rare. The swing between cold and warm is about 16°C, and that helps the grapes ripen.
Rain is fairly plentiful, about 793 mm a year on average. It falls unevenly: October to December are the wettest months and June to August the driest.

Sun adds to it. July and August average more than 300 hours of sun, which is exceptional for this latitude and for the Atlantic-influenced northwest. The grapes ripen slowly, and slow ripening builds the colour and the aromas of the wines.

chapters.title: Slate, quartzite and a thirsty clay
paras: The soils are a mix of quartzite, sandstone, limestone, clay and slate. Their texture is franco-arcillosa, a clay loam, which passes water to the vines when they need it most. They are brown when dry and reddish-brown when wet.

They are acid, with no carbonates, and hold a lot of water. Their humus comes from the old forest and scrub that once covered the basin. They are low in organic matter, which favours quality over quantity.
More coarse slate and quartzite in the loam brings elegance and fineness to the wines. That is what sets them apart from wines of other zones.

chapters.title: Old vines, small harvests
paras: Monks and farmers have shaped Bierzo's local grapes for centuries. 25 monasteries are documented in the area before the desamortización, the sale of church lands. Mencía makes up about 75% of the vines, and Godello is the other main grape.

The average vine is about 75 years old, and old vineyards cover 85% of the vine area. Many were planted from the late 19th century into the early 20th century. Old vines carry many pruning scars that slow the sap. They make fewer and smaller bunches, with more sugar in the grapes.

Narrow planting and steep slopes, once worked by animals, keep yields modest. Mencía is capped at 11,000 kg per hectare, and no more than 81.40 hl per hectare of wine can be made from it. Irrigation is generally forbidden, except to keep vines alive or to improve grape quality.
The result is red wine with lots of fruit that can age in barrel, and white wine that is fresh, tasty and full-bodied.
